findings.title: Unauthenticated API endpoints in web frontend
findings.description: Multiple SvelteKit API routes lack any authentication mechanism. The endpoints /chat, /api/youtube/transcript, /obsidian, and /notes are publicly accessible with no API key, session, or token validation. This allows unauthorized users to consume backend resources, call external APIs (YouTube transcripts), execute Fabric patterns, and write arbitrary files to the server filesystem.

findings.title: Arbitrary file write vulnerability in /notes endpoint
findings.description: The /notes endpoint (web/src/routes/notes/+server.ts) writes user-supplied filename and content directly to the filesystem without validation. An attacker can use path traversal (e.g., '../../../etc/passwd') to write files outside the intended directory. No checks on filename format, content type, or file size. File permissions set to world-readable (0644).

locations.snippet:
const inboxPath = join(__dirname, '...', 'myfiles', 'inbox', filename);
await writeFile(inboxPath, content, 'utf-8');

findings.title: Command injection vulnerability in /obsidian endpoint
findings.description: The /obsidian endpoint uses shell command execution (execAsync) with user-supplied input. Although the code attempts to escape shell arguments via escapeShellArg(), the function only escapes single quotes and may miss edge cases. The mkdir, echo, cp, ls, and wc commands execute user content. Attacker can craft malicious 'noteName' or 'content' values to break out of quotes and execute arbitrary commands.

findings.title: Missing API key authentication on Go REST API backend
findings.description: The Go backend implements APIKeyMiddleware in internal/server/auth.go (line 11-35) but exempt Swagger documentation endpoints from auth (/swagger/*). However, no evidence that this middleware is actually applied to protected routes in the server setup. The middleware exists but may not be enforced on all handlers, particularly the sessions and patterns endpoints that manage user data. No mention of auth enforcement in handler registration code.

locations.snippet: func APIKeyMiddleware(apiKey string) gin.HandlerFunc { ... if strings.HasPrefix(c.Request.URL.Path, "/swagger/") { c.Next() return } ... }
type SessionsHandler struct { ... } func NewSessionsHandler(r *gin.Engine, sessions *fsdb.SessionsEntity) { ... } // No evidence of middleware applied

findings.title: GitHub token exposure in environment variable and CLI flag
findings.description: GitHub API tokens are passed via environment variable GITHUB_TOKEN and CLI flag --token in cmd/generate_changelog/main.go and cmd/generate_changelog/util/token.go. While the token is loaded from environment (checking GITHUB_TOKEN and GH_TOKEN), the token value may be logged, printed to stdout, or stored in plaintext .env files. The .env file loaded in main.go (line 75-80) stores the token on disk with default 0644 permissions (world-readable).

locations.snippet: if err := godotenv.Load(envPath); err != nil { fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Warning: Failed to load .env file: %v\n", err) }
func GetTokenFromEnv(tokenValue string) string { if tokenValue == "" { tokenValue = os.Getenv("GITHUB_TOKEN") ... } return tokenValue }
rootCmd.Flags().StringVar(&cfg.GitHubToken, "token", "", "GitHub API token (or set GITHUB_TOKEN env var")

findings.title: Hardcoded API endpoint without TLS verification
findings.description: The chat endpoint in web/src/routes/chat/+server.ts hardcodes localhost:8080 backend address (line 78) without verifying HTTPS or TLS. This is acceptable for development but dangerous in production. No certificate pinning or validation. If the frontend is served over HTTPS but backend communication is HTTP, this creates a mixed-content vulnerability and allows MITM attacks on sensitive chat data.

locations.snippet: const fabricResponse = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/api/chat', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(body) });

findings.title: Session state stored entirely on client side without integrity protection
findings.description: Sessions in the web frontend (web/src/lib/store/session-store.ts and related components) appear to load session history from API endpoints (lines 23-62 in session-store.ts) but the session selector allows arbitrary user input for session names with no server-side validation. A user can request any session name and retrieve its data. There is no CSRF token protection, no signature verification, and sessions are tied only to a session name string.

locations.snippet: async loadSessions() { const response = await fetch(`/api/sessions/names`); ... const response = await fetch(`/api/sessions/${name}`); }
const messages = await sessionAPI.loadSessionMessages(sessionInput); messageStore.set(messages);

findings.title: Missing input validation on pattern execution
findings.description: The chat endpoint accepts user input (body.prompts[0].userInput, body.messages) and forwards it directly to the Go backend without validation. No checks for command injection, malicious patterns, size limits, or content type. User can send extremely large payloads, special characters, or control sequences that may break pattern parsing on the backend.

locations.snippet: const body = await request.json(); ... console.log('3. Full request:', JSON.stringify(body, null, 2)); const fabricResponse = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/api/chat', { ... body: JSON.stringify(body) });

findings.title: Session files stored on disk with default permissions
findings.description: Session data is stored as JSON files in ~/.config/fabric/sessions (via internal/plugins/db/fsdb/sessions.go). The SaveSession function (line 22) saves to disk but there is no mention of file permission restrictions. Sessions may contain sensitive chat history and AI-generated content. If file permissions default to world-readable (0644), other users on the system can read session data.

locations.snippet: func (o *SessionsEntity) SaveSession(session *Session) (err error) { return o.SaveAsJson(session.Name, session.Messages) }

findings.title: No rate limiting on API endpoints
findings.description: The web API endpoints (/chat, /api/youtube/transcript, /obsidian, /notes) have no rate limiting. An attacker can make unlimited requests to consume backend resources, call expensive YouTube API repeatedly, or fill disk space with arbitrarily named files via the /obsidian endpoint.

findings.title: Verbose error messages exposing system details
findings.description: Error responses return detailed error messages and stack traces (web/src/routes/chat/+server.ts line 120-130, obsidian/+server.ts line 84-93). In production, detailed error messages can leak information about system architecture, file paths, backend dependencies, and API keys.

locations.snippet: return json( { error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Failed to process request' }, { status: 500 } );
return json( { error: error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Failed to process request', details: error instanceof Error ? error.stack : undefined }, { status: 500 } );

findings.title: Missing abstraction layer between web routes and AI providers
findings.description: Web API routes (web/src/routes/chat/+server.ts, web/src/routes/api/youtube/transcript/+server.ts, web/src/routes/obsidian/+server.ts) directly instantiate and call AI provider implementations. This creates tight coupling between request handlers and provider logic, making it difficult to swap providers or add new ones without modifying route handlers.

locations.snippet: Web API route handling chat requests directly calling AI provider logic
YouTube transcript route directly instantiating transcript service
Obsidian integration route with mixed concerns

findings.suggested_fix: Create an abstraction layer (AIFacade or ProviderFactory) that web routes depend on. This layer should handle provider selection, instantiation, and fallback logic. Update routes to call this facade instead of provider implementations directly.

findings.title: God module: cmd/generate_changelog/ mixes concerns across 16 files with 800 LOC
findings.description: The changelog generator contains multiple responsibility domains spread across files: git operations (walker.go, 582 LOC), GitHub API client (client.go, 431 LOC), changelog generation (generator.go, 806 LOC), processing (processing.go, 544 LOC), caching (cache.go, 485 LOC). These should be organized into distinct packages with clear boundaries rather than bundled under a single command.

locations.snippet: Git walking and commit analysis logic
GitHub API client with authentication and PR/release fetching
Main changelog generation orchestrator
Changelog processing and merge detection
SQLite caching layer for performance

findings.suggested_fix: Reorganize into separate internal packages: 'internal/vcs' for git operations, 'internal/github' for GitHub API, 'internal/generator' for changelog generation, 'internal/cache' for persistence. Each should have a clear interface and minimal cross-dependencies.

findings.title: Inconsistent authentication patterns between CLI and web interface
findings.description: CLI commands (fabric-cli, code2context, etc.) authenticate via environment variables (API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, etc.), while the web interface has zero authentication at all—all endpoints are completely public. This creates a security inconsistency where the same AI provider credentials can be accessed by any network user via the web interface without authorization.

locations.snippet: No authentication check on POST /chat
No authentication check on /api/youtube/transcript
No authentication check on /obsidian
No authentication check on /notes

findings.suggested_fix: Implement consistent authentication across web routes. Add middleware for auth token validation, API key validation, or session management. Consider adding optional auth_required flag to route handlers. Document the security model clearly.

findings.title: Tight coupling: web frontend services depend directly on API endpoints without abstraction
findings.description: Web services (ChatService.ts, transcriptService.ts, PdfConversionService.ts) make HTTP calls directly to specific route paths hardcoded in base.ts. There is no API client abstraction or versioning layer, making refactoring API routes difficult without updating multiple service files.

locations.snippet: ChatService making direct HTTP calls to /chat endpoint
TranscriptService with hardcoded API path
Base API client with hardcoded endpoints

findings.suggested_fix: Create an APIClient abstraction layer that centralizes all endpoint definitions. Use configuration-driven endpoint mapping. Consider using a client code generator if the API grows further.

findings.title: Missing service layer in web application: business logic scattered across components and stores
findings.description: Web components (Chat.svelte, ChatInput.svelte, ChatMessages.svelte) directly access stores and make API calls. There is no service layer to encapsulate business logic like session management, context handling, or message processing. This violates separation of concerns and makes testing difficult.

locations.snippet: Chat component with mixed UI and business logic
ChatInput component directly manipulating stores and making API calls
Chat store handling state without clear separation

findings.suggested_fix: Extract business logic into dedicated service classes (ChatSessionService, MessageProcessingService). Have components call services instead of directly manipulating stores. Update stores to be reactive state containers only.

findings.title: Configuration scatter: hardcoded values and settings spread across multiple files
findings.description: Configuration values are scattered throughout the codebase: API endpoints in base.ts, feature flags in config/features.ts, environment settings in config/environment.ts, model configurations in multiple places, and pattern defaults in internal/tools/defaults.go. There is no centralized configuration system.

locations.snippet: Environment configuration
Feature flags
API endpoint configuration
Pattern and tool defaults

findings.suggested_fix: Create a unified configuration system (e.g., config.ts for web, config.go for CLI) that loads from environment, config files, or defaults. Use a configuration object accessible throughout the app. Document all configuration options.

findings.title: Inconsistent error handling and logging patterns across Go modules
findings.description: Different Go packages use different error handling approaches: some return errors directly, some wrap with context, some use panic. The logging module (internal/log/) exists but is not consistently used across all packages. This makes debugging and monitoring difficult.

locations.snippet: Logger implementation not uniformly used
Git walker with inconsistent error handling
GitHub client with different error patterns

findings.suggested_fix: Establish error handling and logging conventions: use structured logging throughout, wrap errors with context using fmt.Errorf with %w, establish panic policies (avoid in libraries), add middleware for consistent logging in handlers.

findings.title: High coupling: AI provider implementations tightly bound to CLI and web interfaces
findings.description: AI provider packages (internal/plugins/ai/openai/, internal/plugins/ai/anthropic/, etc.) are directly imported and instantiated by CLI commands (internal/cli/chat.go) and web routes without using a factory or registry pattern. Adding a new provider requires modifying multiple entry points.

locations.snippet: CLI chat command directly importing specific AI providers
Plugin registry with large hardcoded provider list

findings.suggested_fix: The codebase already has a plugin registry (plugin_registry.go). Ensure all AI provider instantiation goes through this registry. Make the registry configuration-driven to allow adding providers without code changes.

findings.title: Missing layering: web routes directly access file system and perform I/O without abstraction
findings.description: Routes like /obsidian/+server.ts and /notes/+server.ts directly access the file system and parse markdown. There is no persistence abstraction layer or repository pattern to isolate I/O operations from request handlers.

locations.snippet: Obsidian route with direct file system access
Notes route accessing files directly

findings.suggested_fix: Create abstraction layers: NoteRepository for file operations, ObsidianVaultAdapter for Obsidian-specific logic. Have routes depend on these abstractions, not on direct file I/O.

findings.title: Circular dependencies risk: tool-specific code in internal/tools/ may depend on core plugins
findings.description: The internal/tools/ package contains multiple tool implementations (youtube.go, spotify.go, jina.go) that may create circular import chains if core plugin systems depend on them while they depend on plugin registries.

locations.snippet: YouTube tool with 841 LOC
Spotify tool with 525 LOC
Plugin registry managing tool registration

findings.suggested_fix: Verify import paths are acyclic. Use a dependency graph tool to validate. Consider whether tools belong in core or should be separate plugins. Document the intended dependency direction.

items.title: Implement authentication for all web API endpoints

API key validation uses environment variable API_KEY or similar

items.approach: Create src/hooks.server.ts with auth middleware that intercepts all protected routes. Extract API key from environment. Validate on every request before handler execution.

items.approach: Add input validation before writeFile: sanitize with basename(), validate regex, check size, verify resolved path. Use path.resolve() to detect escapes.

items.title: Replace shell execution with Node.js APIs in /obsidian endpoint

File operations use fs/promises (writeFile, mkdir, etc.)
noteName sanitized with basename() and regex validation

Path traversal tests pass

items.approach: Replace all exec() calls with Node.js fs APIs. Sanitize noteName using basename and regex. Use path.resolve() to validate final path.

remediation_plan.dedup_summary: Merged F-d1a8e2f6 (unauthenticated endpoints) with F-4db5d358 (inconsistent auth patterns) into single auth implementation task. Deduplication addressed overlapping findings on input validation (F-73bb561e reuses patterns from F-5e7ef160 and F-deb91026). Error message sanitization (F-d9127866) and logging standardization (F-bec044cf) handled as separate concerns but coordinated. Architecture findings (F-c7786f89, F-cea458fb, F-5aa62f1e, F-12a57dae) ordered by dependencies rather than merged.
remediation_plan.summary: 21 remediation items across 4 execution levels. Level 0 (10 items): Critical auth and secrets fixes, 3 days. Level 1 (6 items): Input validation, CSRF, rate limiting, 2 days. Level 2 (3 items): File security and abstraction layers, 2 days. Level 3 (2 items): Major refactoring (changelog reorganization, service extraction), 3 days. Total estimated effort: 10 days for team of 2 engineers. No items deferred; all critical security and architectural issues addressed.

codebase_map.architecture_summary: A multi-tool AI CLI application written in Go with a SvelteKit web frontend. The core functionality uses pattern-based AI prompting (200+ patterns in data/patterns/) to analyze, extract, summarize, and transform text content. Supports multiple AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, AWS Bedrock, Perplexity, Google Gemini). Includes auxiliary tools for changelog generation, code context extraction, and PDF conversion. The web interface provides a chat UI and pattern browsing. All AI calls are authenticated via environment API keys; the web interface has no authentication layer.
